title: Research or a faster prototype
excerpt: Talk to users when you are guessing the job. Prototype when you already know the job and need to see the interface. Do not research only to delay a decision.
alt: Smooth overlapping waves of blue, violet, and warm orange, a form you can judge by looking once the job is known.
caption: A form you can judge by looking. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a team talk to users before designing?
faqs.answer: Talk to them when you cannot agree on the job, or when recent sales calls describe different tasks. Ask people to walk through the last time they did the work. Stop when the same stall shows up again and you can write the job in their verbs.

faqs.question: When is a prototype the better next step?
faqs.answer: Build a prototype when you already know the user, the task, and the constraint, and you need to see whether the interface makes that job obvious. Include the empty state, one real error, and the phone frame. Use real words, not placeholder labels.

faqs.question: What is a research phase that is really a delay?
faqs.answer: It is a plan with weeks of interviews and no date on which a screen will exist, or a pile of personas that do not change the interface. Set the decision date before the first conversation. Research can show you the jobs. You still have to choose one.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
When to skip user research is a narrower question than the slogans suggest. Talk to users when you are guessing the job: who it is for, what they are trying to do, and what they already use. Build a prototype when you already know the job and you need to see whether the interface makes that job visible. A research phase that exists so nobody has to decide is a delay. Name it as a delay and stop.

The two activities answer different questions. Mixing them up produces either a thick report and no page, or a polished prototype of a guess.

## When you are guessing the job

You are guessing when the team cannot agree on the user without inventing them, or when the last five sales calls described five different tasks. You are guessing when "everyone" is the answer to "who is this for." You are guessing when the feature list is a catalog of competitors and nobody has watched a person fail.

In that state, a prototype will only make the guess look expensive. Talk to people first. A small number is enough if you are actually listening. Five to eight conversations with people who have the job, not with friends who are being kind. Ask them to walk through the last time they did the task. What they opened, where they stalled, what they used instead.

Write down the job in their verbs. "Send the signed agreement before the courier leaves" is a job. "Empower teams" is not. If you cannot fill a page with verbs, you do not know enough to draw.

Do not outsource the listening so completely that the founder only reads a summary. The founder is the one who will refuse a feature later. They should hear the stall in the customer's voice at least a few times. A studio can run the sessions and keep them honest. The notes should be quotes and steps, not a slide of personas with stock faces.

Stop the research when the job repeats. When the fourth conversation describes the same stall as the second, you are learning less than you think. Write the job at the top of a page and move to the interface. More interviews after that are a way to avoid drawing.

## When you already know the job

You know the job when you can say the user, the task, and the constraint without looking at a deck. You have done the work yourself, or you have sold it, or you have sat next to someone who does it every day. The remaining question is whether a stranger can see that job in the interface.

That question is answered by a prototype, not by another interview about feelings. Draw the path. The first screen says the job. The next step is the thing they came to do. The empty state tells the truth. Put it in Figma, or in the browser if the interaction is the point. Hanabi's production interfaces are built in React and TypeScript. The prototype does not have to be that code on day one. It has to be faithful to the path, including the ugly step you are tempted to hide.

Watch someone use it without your narration. Sit still. The places they hesitate are the design. The places they understand are done. You do not need a lab. A video call and a shared screen are enough if you can keep yourself from explaining.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research on page time](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the reason a clear prototype still has to say the right job. People often decide to leave in the first 10 seconds, and a page only earns a longer look when the value is visible in that window. A beautiful prototype of the wrong job will be clear and still fail. Speed does not repair a bad target. It publishes the bad target faster. Get the job right, then use the prototype to see if the page can say it in that short window.

## Research as a way to avoid a decision

The tell is the plan. Six weeks of interviews, a workshop, a journey map, and no date on which a screen will exist. The team calls it rigor. Often it is fear of choosing a user and being wrong in public.

Research cannot choose for you. It can show you the jobs that exist. You still pick which job this product will do. If you are waiting for a finding that removes the responsibility, you will commission another round. Set the decision date before the first call. On that date, write the job you are building, including the jobs you are leaving out.

A second tell: the research is aimed at the founder's anxiety rather than a question. "Will people like it?" is not a question you can answer in advance. "Where do they stall when they export?" is a question. If you cannot form the second kind, you are not ready to hire a researcher. You are ready to name the product.

A studio should refuse a research phase whose deliverable is only permission. On a Hanabi project the useful output is a sentence and a path: who it is for, what they do, what the interface must show. If the engagement cannot produce those, it is the wrong engagement, whether it is called research or discovery.

Skip the theater. Competitive screenshots are not research. A persona with a name and a hobby is not research. A survey of people who are not the user is not research. These artifacts photograph well in a deck and do not change the interface. If you need two days to align the team, call it an alignment workshop. Do not call it user research.

## What the prototype has to show

A faster prototype is not a prettier one. It has to show the decision.

- The first screen, with the job in a sentence a stranger can read without you.
- The primary path, clicked or tapped, including the step you find embarrassing.
- The empty state, before they have data.
- One error that actually happens.
- The phone frame, because that is where the path often breaks.

Leave out the illustration pass, the motion study, and the alternate homepage. Those are how a prototype becomes a brand exercise. You are trying to learn whether the job is visible. Motion in the Motion library, or a Framer preview, can wait until the path is right. If a transition is the product, prototype that transition and nothing else.

Put real words in it. Lorem and "feature one" teach you nothing. Use the sentence from the research, or from the sales call if you skipped research because you already knew. If the words do not fit the component, the component is wrong or the words are. That is the lesson. Do not solve it by shrinking the type until the lie fits.

Show it to someone who will use it, and to someone who will build it. The user tells you if the job is recognizable. The engineer tells you if the path is a fantasy. Both conversations are short when the prototype is small. A huge prototype makes both conversations political, because too much work is at stake to admit the first screen is wrong.

## A small research pass

When you do need to talk to people, keep the pass small enough to finish.

1. Write the question. One question. "What happens today when they need X?"
2. List eight people who do that. Expect to reach five.
3. Hold the conversations in a week. Record them if they agree. Take notes in their words.
4. On the last day, write the job, the stall, and what you will not build.
5. Start the prototype the next morning.

If you cannot list eight people, you may not have access to the user yet. Fix that before you hire a research practice. The founder's network, the current customers, and the people who wrote in and were rejected are the list. A recruited panel of strangers can help later, when the question is about a detail. It is a poor way to discover whether the company should exist.

Pay people for their time when the conversation is more than a favor. You will listen differently, and they will show up. Do not pay them to praise the idea. Ask for the walkthrough of the real task. Praise is cheap and it does not draw a screen.

Share the notes with the whole team that will build. A research summary that lives in one person's drive is how the guess returns. The job statement should be short enough to paste at the top of the prototype file.

## What to do with what you learn

Change the sentence, the user, or the path. If you change nothing, you did not learn, or you are ignoring what you heard. Write the change in one paragraph so the next person can see it. "We thought the job was reporting. The job is sending the file before 4pm. The homepage will start there."

Kill a feature if the conversations never reached it. A feature nobody mentioned and nobody stalled on is a feature you wanted to build. Put it on a later list. Do not put it on the first prototype out of attachment.

Then build the smallest real version of the path you kept. A prototype that never becomes a page is a rehearsal. The point of skipping the extra research was to get to the interface. Ship the interface to the people you spoke with, if they are your users, and watch the same path again in production. The second watch is worth more than a second report.

If the thing you need next is not a research plan but a page for a specific day, the constraints get even tighter. One page, one offer, one way to meet, for a person who heard the name once. That is the conference problem, and it is next: [the site you need before a conference](/blog/the-site-you-need-before-a-conference).

When the job is known and you want the prototype built rather than left in a file, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).
